findings.explanation:
Two requirements, two interfaces. Aggregating across more than 50,000 Contacts needs Batch Apex, because Database.Batchable is what splits the work into chunks — the per-transaction limits reset for each execute() call, so the job never meets the 50,000-record query-row ceiling that a single transaction would hit. Running it once a day after hours needs Schedulable, which is what System.schedule() takes and what lets you set the time. The two go together: the Schedulable class's execute() calls Database.executeBatch() on the Batchable class.
Queueable will not carry the volume. A queueable job runs as one transaction with one set of governor limits, so aggregating every Contact runs into the same 50,000-row query limit that ordinary Apex does; it also has no scheduling of its own. The @future annotation is weaker still — it can't be scheduled, returns no job id, can't be chained, and takes only primitives and collections of primitives as arguments. Note that the well-known 50 attached to @future is the maximum number of future methods allowed per Apex invocation, not a cap on records per call.
One detail that catches people out: scheduled Apex is asynchronous, but synchronous governor limits apply to a scheduled job. So Schedulable on its own does not buy you extra headroom — that is exactly why the Batchable half of the answer is needed and not optional.

Aggregating across more than 50,000 Contacts needs Database.Batchable, because Batch Apex splits the work into chunks and the per-transaction limits reset for each execute() call, so the job never meets the 50,000-record query-row ceiling a single transaction would hit. Running it once a day after hours needs Schedulable, which is what System.schedule() takes; its execute() then calls Database.executeBatch() on the Batchable class.
Queueable will not carry the volume: a queueable job runs as one transaction with one set of governor limits, so aggregating every Contact meets the same 50,000-row query limit ordinary Apex does, and it has no scheduling of its own. The @future annotation is weaker still — it can't be scheduled, returns no job id, can't be chained, and accepts only primitives and collections of primitives as arguments, so you can't even hand it a list of sObjects.
Be careful with the number 50 here. Execution Governors and Limits gives it as the maximum number of methods with the future annotation allowed per Apex invocation — a cap on how many future calls one transaction can make. It is not a limit on how many records a future method may process.
Also worth knowing: scheduled Apex is an asynchronous feature, but synchronous governor limits apply to a scheduled job. Schedulable alone therefore buys no extra headroom, which is precisely why the Batchable half of the answer is required.
findings.note: Answer C,D stands. The explanation invented a governor limit: it stated that @future "has a limit of 50 records per method call". No such limit exists — Execution Governors and Limits gives 50 as the maximum number of methods with the future annotation allowed per Apex invocation. Rewritten with the real constraints on @future (no scheduling, no job id, no chaining, primitive-only arguments) and with the documented note that synchronous limits apply to scheduled Apex, which is the actual reason Schedulable alone is insufficient.
